Action Plan:
1. Immediate emergency response: Patient’s wife instructed to call an ambulance (000) for urgent transfer to hospital due to suspected early anaphylaxis after wasp sting.  
2. Interim home treatment: Patient advised to take an oral antihistamine available at home while awaiting ambulance arrival.  
3. Hospital care: ED team to assess airway, breathing, circulation; be prepared to administer intramuscular adrenaline, oxygen, IV fluids, corticosteroids, additional antihistamines as per anaphylaxis protocol.  
4. Post-discharge preventive measures (to be addressed after acute episode): arrange prescription and education for self-injectable adrenaline (e.g., EpiPen; dose/route/frequency not documented) and referral to allergy clinic for venom immunotherapy consideration.  
5. Safety netting: Patient advised that symptoms can worsen rapidly; if breathing becomes more difficult, lip/throat swelling increases, or dizziness develops before ambulance arrival, call 999 again and use adrenaline autoinjector if available (none on hand).  
6. Documentation/consent: Verbal consent from patient has been obtained before using transcription software.

Subjective:
• Presenting complaint: Acute shallow breathing and chest tightness ~15 min after a wasp sting while gardening.  
• Associated symptoms: Tingling sensation in lips, blotchy skin rash. Denies throat closing; no prior similar reaction.  
• Past medical history: Eczema; aerosinusitis with flying.  
• Allergies: Penicillin (type/severity not detailed).  
• Medications: Intermittent antihistamine use for flying; no other regular medicines reported.  
• Social: Married; wife present at home; no smoking/alcohol history provided.

Objective:
• Remote video consult—no vitals or physical exam possible.  
• Patient subjectively reports shallow breathing, chest tightness, lip tingling, blotchy rash. No visualised lip swelling or audible wheeze documented.  
• No investigations performed.

Assessment & Plan:

1. Acute breathing difficulty after wasp sting  
   - Assessment / likely diagnosis: Suspected anaphylaxis secondary to wasp sting (DDx: “Anaphylaxis secondary to wasp sting” – High).  
   - Differential diagnosis:  
     • Systemic allergic urticaria without full anaphylaxis (Medium) – cutaneous findings but airway signs mild.  
     • Anxiety / panic-induced hyperventilation (Low) – stress related, but rash supports allergic cause.  
     • Asthma/reactive airway exacerbation (Low) – no asthma history, no wheeze (conflict noted: DDx lists as low).  
   - Investigations planned: To be completed in ED – serial vitals, pulse oximetry, ECG, serum tryptase (if indicated).  
   - Treatment planned:  
     • Administer oral antihistamine immediately at home.  
     • Emergency medical services activation and transport to hospital.  
     • Expect ED management per anaphylaxis protocol (IM adrenaline, oxygen, IV fluids, corticosteroids, antihistamines).  
   - Relevant referrals: Post-event referral to allergy/immunology for venom allergy testing and immunotherapy.

Quality checks:
• Missing elements: No objective vitals, physical exam, or medication reconciliation beyond antihistamine; family, occupational, and lifestyle details incomplete.  
• Internal conflicts: None noted between transcript and DDx except low-likelihood asthma listed in DDx though patient reports no asthma history (conflict noted).  
• Transcript quality: Clear; minimal background noise; short consult limited by urgency.
